https://telex.hu/kulfold/2026/09/13/bori.text: Menü Kereső Boris Johnson nem sokkal a támadás előtt ugyanazon az ukrán vasútvonalon utazott, ahol orosz dróntámadás ért egy vonatot Külföld Krász Zsombor Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Boris Johnson korábbi brit miniszterelnök és több magas rangú európai biztonsági tisztviselő nem sokkal azelőtt haladt át a területen, hogy orosz dróntámadás ért vasárnap hajnalban egy személyvonatot az ukrán-lengyel határ közelében – írta meg a BBC. Mint korábban megírtuk, egy orosz drón találta el Ukrajnában a Kijev és Varsó között közlekedő személyszállító vonat mozdonyát akkor, amikor a szerelvény két kilométerre volt a lengyel határtól. A dróntámadásokat felügyelő társaság előre figyelmeztette a vonat személyzetét a fenyegetésre, aminek köszönhetően senki sem sérült meg. A lengyel PKP InterCity vasúttársaság közölte, hogy az utasok között nem voltak lengyel állampolgárok, még azelőtt történt a támadás, mielőtt a PKP InterCity átvette a vonatot. A vonaton 206 utas utazott. A BBC szerint Boris Johnson és más európai nemzetbiztonsági tanácsadók, köztük Jonathan Powell brit kormánytanácsadó egy másik vonaton, de ugyanazon a vonalon utaztak visszafelé egy kijevi konferenciáról, az évente megrendezett Yalta European Strategy-ről, amin politikai, üzleti és biztonsági területen dolgozó vezetők és szakértők vesznek részt. Az eset után Oroszország közölte, hogy csak Ukrajna vasúti infrastruktúráját támadták, de az ukrán állami vasúttársaság, az Ukrzaliznyicja szerint „könnyen lehet, hogy ennek a drónnak a diplomáciai vonat volt a célpontja”. Közleményükben arról írnak, hogy az orosz támadások folyamatos fenyegetése miatt módosították a menetrendet, így a vonat az eredetileg tervezettnél korábban hagyta el az állomást. Az eltalált vonat utasait mindössze 15 perccel az orosz drón támadása előtt utasították evakuálásra. A vasúttársaság szerint David Petraeus volt CIA-igazgató a dróntámadás idején egy másik vonaton tartózkodott a jahodini állomáson. Carl Bildt volt svéd miniszterelnök szintén részt vett a kijevi konferencián, a BBC-nek arról beszélt, hogy az ő vonatán az utazókat felszólították, hogy készüljenek fel az evakuálásra, de később mégis engedélyt kaptak az út folytatására. Egyes beszámolók szerint Bildt ugyanazon a vonaton utazott, mint Johnson, de a brit miniszterelnök ezt nem erősítette meg a BBC-nek. „Nem tudom, milyen eltorzult logika késztette Putyint arra, hogy ma reggel felrobbantson egy álló ukrán mozdonyt a lengyel határon. Ami viszont biztos, hogy ez pontosan az a fajta véletlenszerű és értelmetlen támadás, amit az ukránok nap mint nap elszenvednek – még a polgári vasúti vonalakon is” – írta az X-en az esetre reagálva Boris Johnson. https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.text: Evelina’s foster mother speaks to the 18-year-old, who spent two years with her in Sicily. After being repatriated to Ukraine, Evelina says she begged to go back to Italy View image in fullscreen Evelina’s foster mother speaks to the 18-year-old, who spent two years with her in Sicily. After being repatriated to Ukraine, Evelina says she begged to go back to Italy Ukraine in depth Global development ‘My future is in the EU’: the Ukrainian children who don’t want to go home Thousands of children in state care were evacuated when Russia invaded. Kyiv wants them back – but many resist Supported by About this content Stefania D'Ignoti. Photographs by Camilla Minnozz Wed 16 Sep 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 06.12 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google W hen he first arrived in his new home in a small village in the Italian Alps in March 2022, 15-year-old Denys* says he felt homesick and confused. He had been put on an overnight bus and relocated along with more than 100 other children from his orphanage in Berdiansk, in eastern Ukraine , which was one of the first areas to be invaded by Russian troops. “Ukraine was all I knew,” says Denys. “I had never left it my whole life.” But after he began going to school, making friends and integrating into Italian life, Denys says he no longer wanted to go back home. “I started to realise there was a different way of life I could be living,” he says. “One that didn’t involve airstrikes and poverty, and that could give me better opportunities for my future.” Thousands of Ukrainian social orphans – children given up to the state or taken away from parents considered unable to care for them – were evacuated overseas after Russia’s invasion in 2022. The relocation was meant to be temporary, but even after the situation stabilised in parts of Ukraine, many of them, such as Denys, refused to return. Ukrainian officials have repatriated most of the children, but more than 1,500 remain elsewhere in Europe. Some – like Denys – have been aided by Italian courts after their foster parents in Italy defied Kyiv’s repatriation order , citing concerns regarding the children’s wellbeing in a war-torn country with heavily damaged social welfare and public infrastructure. For Ukraine, already battling a plummeting birthrate and the loss of children abducted by Russia in occupied territories , the failure of some juveniles to return home has become a crisis. Kateryna Rashevska, a legal expert on war crimes against children in Ukraine, says: “We are losing those who should’ve been the future citizens of our nation. If these children ever actually return to Ukraine, they will have limited Ukrainian language, culture, history and identity, which also poses a threat to our future heritage and demography.” View image in fullscreen Ukrainian teenagers at schools in Rota d’Imagna have weekly online Ukrainian language classes, which is a requirement of the authorities in Kyiv The situation escalated in April after a 15-year-old boy who had been evacuated to Italy in 2022 was legally adopted by an Italian family, despite having parents and two sisters back in Ukraine who wanted him to return home. A court in Italy overruled Ukrainian laws – in May 2022, shortly after the war started, Ukraine had suspended international adoptions to prevent trafficking or wrongful adoptions. Yuliya Donnichenko, a Ukrainian national based in Italy who has overseen evacuations to southern Italy and repatriations back to Ukraine for about 100 orphans, says there have been many childless couples who she sensed were taking advantage of the unstable situation to bypass strict international adoption laws and get a Ukrainian child. “I know that they meant the best for these kids, that they became attached to them and wanted the best for their future, away from a war-torn nation. But what they don’t understand is that by [seeking adoption] they’re putting at risk an already fragile situation,” she says. “It might not seem like a lot – just a few more hundreds compared with the already 20,000 lost to Russia – but to us every child counts. It’s the future of our nation.” Some accuse Ukraine of not being prepared to offer stable conditions and a fair future to a new generation, with the reality of return for many of the children different from what they were promised. Evelina, now 18, was repatriated after almost two years spent with an Italian foster family in Sicily, and was assigned to an adoptive Ukrainian family on the border with Romania. The family already had several foster children under their care, making her living conditions “not much different from living in an orphanage”, she says. Evelina says that when she returned home, she had her phone confiscated for more than a year, as she was not allowed to be in touch with the Italian family who hosted her throughout her stay there. “I was confined at home and didn’t go to school. I would only leave my room for an English class once a week or church on Sunday,” she says. “I felt very depressed; I didn’t understand why they made me return to live like this.” View image in fullscreen Almost 100 Ukrainian orphans were evacuated to Rota d’Imagna, in Bergamo, northern Italy When she was finally given a new phone in autumn 2024, Evelina says she managed to open a Telegram account and spent hours talking to her Italian foster mother – the only mental escape from otherwise long, boring days. “I missed her. I constantly begged her to come pick me up and bring me back to Sicily,” she says. Evelina says her new family would record videos of her going up and down the street outside her home, as proof of her doing a minimum amount of exercise and getting out of the house. After she shared her concerns with the Italian family, Evelina’s phone was confiscated again, and her WhatsApp and Telegram accounts were permanently deleted. Now she is 18, Evelina says she cannot wait to leave Ukraine and return to the EU: “It made no sense to force our return since most of us had planned to leave anyway after turning 18, thanks to the connections we developed in Europe . skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every fortnight Sign up to Global Dispatch Get a different world view with a roundup of the best news, features, opinion and photography, curated by our global development team after newsletter promotion “After all,” she says. “It was unfair to pretend we’d just get a quick taste of freedom in Europe and then head back to a place that can’t offer us as much as an EU country can right now.” Denys says he and almost 100 orphans evacuated to Rota d’Imagna, in the hills of Bergamo, received their repatriation order from Kyiv in August 2024. He was 17 at the time of the call to return, which meant that setting foot in Ukraine for him – as well as other boys in his age range – could mean being drafted into the war. “I was utterly frightened, but the authorities didn’t listen to our concerns,” he says. Russia has network of 200 camps for ‘brainwashing’ Ukrainian children – report Read more During one-on-one meetings in Italy with the orphans supposed to return, Denys says Ukrainian social workers would use “intimidating language and even swearwords if we showed any signs of resistance”, with younger ones “promised candies and PlayStations on their arrival in Ukraine”. He says: “They would use any possible, misleading argument to convince us to accept the return. They promised us we’d be adopted or reunited with family relatives we still had back home. All fake promises they couldn’t guarantee for sure.” With the help of Italian courts, Denys managed to stay in Italy, where he now works as a waiter and hopes to remain for the foreseeable future. He says those who ended up returning tell him they regret the choice, and that many stay not with adoptive parents but at institutions where there is no running water or electricity, and where up to six people live in the same room. View image in fullscreen Diego Mosca, who supervised the group of Ukrainian orphans in Rota d’Imagna, says the children had been ‘tossed around like a tennis ball between two sides’ He says they regularly have to hide in bunkers, as even western provinces in Ukraine are targeted by Russian attacks. “This proves that they didn’t have our best interests and safety at heart,” he says. Maksym, another orphan from the Rota d’Imagna group, said he reluctantly accepted repatriation, only to move to Germany three months later when he turned 18. “Ukraine changed too much over the past few years. There’s nothing for us young people there. My future is in the EU.” Diego Mosca, who supervised the group of Ukrainian orphans in Rota d’Imagna, says the children had been “tossed around like a tennis ball between two sides” by the repatriation dispute. “This situation has traumatised them and will forever leave wounds on their psyche. Providing mental health support to those who returned should be a priority over demographic needs.” * Name changed to protect identity Explore more on these topics Global development Ukraine in depth Ukraine Italy Children Europe Adoption Fostering features Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.politico.eu/article/macron-a.text: BRUSSELS — France and Germany said Friday they had struck a deal to favor European-made cars under a landmark EU industry bill in exchange for weakening a 2035 vehicle emissions target, ending months of wrangling between the bloc’s two biggest economies. Under the agreement, Germany would accept stricter “Made in Europe” — or local content — requirements for the automotive industry in the proposed Industrial Accelerator Act, a longstanding French demand, while France would back Berlin’s push to relax the EU’s plan to phase out new combustion-engine cars. The EU’s current target is for companies to reduce emissions from new vehicles by 100% from 2021 levels by 2035, with the possibility to “earn” 10% of emissions leeway through initiatives like offsets and investments. Advertisement Advertisement France and Germany now want to soften the 2035 target to 90% but without having to offer investments in alternative fuels to compensate the remaining 10%, as proposed by the European Commission. “This balanced approach will enable the European Union to pursue its climate objectives while strengthening the technological sovereignty, industrial base and international competitiveness of its automotive industry,” the two countries said in a joint statement . The agreement, first reported by POLITICO in July , was due to have been announced Thursday, during a meeting of EU leaders in Brussels. But it was held up at the last minute by disagreements within Germany’s governing coalition. “We hope that this Franco-German dynamic can swiftly lead to an agreement with our partners, for our jobs and our industry,” French President Emmanuel Macron said in a post on social media. An Elysée official on Friday made clear that, under the Franco-German deal, the scope of Made in Europe for automotive can be extended to the U.K. and Switzerland under certain conditions. — addressing a key concern of Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government ahead of a Nov. 20 U.K.-EU summit in Brussels. The agreement was reached after the German Social Democratic Party, the junior partner in Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s coalition government, dropped its opposition. Advertisement Advertisement “This is a modern realignment of German industrial policy that places significantly greater emphasis on preserving jobs and production sites,” said German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider, who is from the SPD. “The clear expectation for German companies is that they will use these new opportunities to make investments and guarantee jobs here in Germany,” he added. CORRECTION: This article was updated on Oct. 16 after an earlier version misrepresented the figures in the Franco-German proposal on the softening of 2035 targets.
